info.text: Formative quiz for Chapter 14. From Think Python, 3rd edition, by Allen B. Downey (https://allendowney.github.io/ThinkPython/), CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

questiontext.text: To create an instance of a programmer-defined type, what is the correct order for these steps?

answer.text: Assign values to attributes, define a class, instantiate an object.

feedback.text: You can't assign attributes before you instantiate an object.

answer.text: Instantiate an object, define a class, assign values to attributes.

feedback.text: You can't instantiate an object before you define its class.

answer.text: Define a class, assign values to attributes, instantiate an object.

feedback.text: You can't assign attributes before you instantiate an object.

answer.text: Define a class, instantiate an object, assign values to attributes.

feedback.text: You have to define a class, instantiate an object, and assign values to attributes, in that order.

questiontext.text:
These statements are intended to define a Date class and create a Date object. What is wrong with them?

def Date:
    """Represents a day of the year."""

date = Date()
date.year = 2024
date.month = 'January'
date.day = 11

answer.text: You can't have a class named Date and a variable named date.

feedback.text: It is legal -- and common -- for a class name and a variable to be the same word, but the class name starts with an uppercase letter.

answer.text: All of the attributes have to have the same type.

feedback.text: The attributes of an object can be any type, and they don't have to be the same.

answer.text: The syntax is not correct for adding attributes to the object.

feedback.text: Dot notation is used to set the value of an attribute and to read the value.

answer.text: A class definition has to start with class, not def.

feedback.text: A class definition has to start with class. A function definition starts with def.

questiontext.text:
Which of these is a correct description of this function? You can assume that date is a Date object that has a day attribute.

def increment_day(date):
    date.day += 1
    return date

answer.text: It is a pure function that returns None.

feedback.text: This function modifies an attribute of the Date object it gets as a parameter, so it is an impure function. And it returns a reference to the same object, not None.

answer.text: It is an impure function that returns None.

feedback.text: This function returns a reference to a Date object, not None.

answer.text: It is a pure function that returns a Date object.

feedback.text: This function modifies an attribute of the Date object it gets as a parameter, so it is an impure function.

answer.text: It is an impure function that returns a Date object.

feedback.text: This function modifies an attribute of the Date object it gets as a parameter, so it is an impure function -- and it returns a reference to the same Date object.

questiontext.text:
Suppose today refers to a Date object, and we run this code:

def set_date(date, val):
    date.date = val

set_date(today, 27)

Which of these is true afterward?

answer.text: It caused an error, because date is already the name of a parameter.

feedback.text: A parameter and an attribute can have the same name without conflict: the parameter is a variable in the function's frame and the attribute belongs to the object.
The function never assigns a new value to today or to date; it assigns to an attribute of the object they both refer to.

answer.text: The parameter date was changed to 27, but today is unchanged.

feedback.text: date.date = val does not change the parameter date -- it still refers to the Date object -- and because date and today refer to the same object, the change is visible through today.

answer.text: The Date object that today refers to has an attribute called date whose value is 27.

feedback.text: Inside the function, date refers to the same object as today, so date.date = val creates an attribute of that object. Functions like make_time in this chapter use the same names for parameters and attributes on purpose.
